# Appeal of Denied Prior Authorization — Hip Arthroscopy (CPT 29914)

**Governing Policy:** Aetna CPB 0736 - Hip Preservation Surgery (https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/700_799/0736.html; last review 07/31/2026)

**RE:**
- Member: Taylor Foster
- Member ID: W492196775
- Denial date: 2026-08-24
- Reference number: POC-C65CA65DA3-33163
- Payer/Plan: Aetna (Commercial/ACA), Wyoming
- Requested service: Hip arthroscopy, CPT 29914

Dear Aetna Appeals Department,

I am appealing the denial of prior authorization for my hip arthroscopy (CPT 29914). My surgeon, Dr. Okafor, has documented that this procedure is medically necessary, and I am asking Aetna to reconsider its decision.

## Why I am appealing

The denial states that my records do not document an adequate trial of conservative treatment before surgery. I do not believe this reflects the full record that was submitted, and I want to walk through what my chart actually shows.

### What my records document

- **Symptom duration:** I have had progressive hip pain for 24 months, unrelieved by rest.
- **Physical therapy:** I completed 18 supervised physical therapy visits over 14 weeks (2026-04-27 to 2026-08-03), focused on core and hip stabilization with activity modification. This is documented in my physical therapy discharge note.
- **Medication:** I took NSAIDs for 8 months with inadequate relief.
- **Injection:** I received a corticosteroid injection on 2026-06-14, which gave only 4 weeks of partial relief.
- **Imaging:** An MRI arthrogram on 2026-07-11 showed an anterosuperior labral tear with cam-type femoroacetabular impingement, alpha angle 68 degrees, joint space preserved, Tonnis grade 0.
- **Function and exam:** I have sharp anterior groin pain with sitting and pivoting, cannot run or squat, and had positive provocative testing on the affected side with range of motion limited by pain.

### Mapping to the plan's own policy

The excerpts of CPB 0736 that I have been given describe medical necessity criteria for pelvic osteotomy (PAO) for acetabular dysplasia, and note that arthroscopic surgery is assessed under separate criteria within the same policy. The policy states:

> "Arthroscopic surgery in concert with an osteotomy would be assessed using the medical necessity criteria noted above for arthroscopic surgery of the hip."

This confirms that Aetna's own policy applies a distinct set of medical-necessity criteria to arthroscopic hip surgery. I was not provided with the specific text of those arthroscopy criteria, so I am not able to quote them here, and I want to be transparent about that rather than guess at their wording.

What I can point to is that, elsewhere in this same policy, Aetna sets a duration threshold for conservative treatment before surgical intervention:

> "and Minimum 6 months of symptoms;"

My symptoms have been present for 24 months — four times that threshold — and I have completed a structured, supervised physical therapy program (18 visits over 14 weeks), 8 months of NSAID therapy, and a corticosteroid injection, all without lasting relief. I am asking Aetna to review the specific arthroscopy criteria set out in CPB 0736 against this record, since the treatment history documented by my providers is substantial and well past any 6-month threshold referenced elsewhere in this policy.

I also note that my policy states:

> "These supplemental medical necessity criteria are based upon evidence-based guidelines and clinical studies in the peer-reviewed published medical literature."

I trust that a full review of my chart against those specific arthroscopy criteria — rather than a general finding that conservative care was inadequate — will show that my treatment history meets what the policy requires.

## What I am asking

I am asking Aetna to reconsider the denial of CPT 29914 in light of the conservative treatment I have already completed, and to explain clearly which specific criteria in CPB 0736 my records do not meet, with reference to the actual policy language for arthroscopic hip surgery, if the denial is upheld.

I understand this appeal must be received by **2027-02-20**. I will submit it using Aetna's Member Complaint and Appeal Form (available in my account at aetna.com, under complaints, grievances and appeals), and I will fax or mail it to the address printed on my denial letter, and/or fax it to 859-425-3379. I may also call 1-800-872-3862 or the number on my member ID card with questions.

Thank you for reconsidering my case.

Sincerely,

[Signature]
Taylor Foster
Member ID: W492196775
Date: [date]
Phone: [phone number]
Email: [email address]

---

*This letter is not medical or legal advice and does not guarantee that coverage will be approved.*

quotes: Aetna considers pelvic osteotomy (e.g., peri-acetabular osteotomy (PAO)) medically necessary for a diagnosis of acetabular dysplasia (not borderline dysplasia) for persons who fulfill all of the following criteria:
Aetna considers pelvic osteotomy in skeletally immature children medically necessary for a diagnosis of acetabular dysplasia.
Medically Necessary Procedures Medically necessary procedures, when above criteria are met, include:

Endoscopic tenotomy (or lengthening) for iliopsoas tendinopathy following total hip arthroplasty with the failure of at least 6 weeks of formal in-person physical therapy in the past year, and at least 1 therapeutic injection (steroid with or without local anesthetic) with significant but temporary benefit in the past 6 months.
Repair of complete gluteus medius tears is considered medically necessary.
for members with moderate or worse arthritis (Tonnis 2 or 3), the procedure would be considered not medically necessary;
Arthroscopic surgery in concert with an osteotomy would be assessed using the medical necessity criteria noted above for arthroscopic surgery of the hip.

The supplemental medical necessity criteria in this CPB further define those indications for services that are proven safe and effective where those indications are not fully established in applicable NCDs and LCDs.
These supplemental medical necessity criteria are based upon evidence-based guidelines and clinical studies in the peer-reviewed published medical literature.

The background section of this CPB includes an explanation of the rationale that supports adoption of the medical necessity criteria and a summary of evidence that was considered during the development of the CPB;

While there is a possible risk of reduced or delayed care with any coverage criteria, Aetna believes that the benefits of these criteria – ensuring patients receive services that are appropriate, safe, and effective – substantially outweigh any clinical harms.
